A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same matrix-vector multiplication work. All 36 pages of v1 and 32 pages of v3, including appendices, equations, algorithms and v3's figures, support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports theoretical algorithms, bounds and proofs. Empirical observations about practical efficiency and graph VC-dimensions are attributed to earlier works; no original experiments appear in its appendices.

after.justification: Appendix E reports original simulations on synthetic 4096-by-4096 Boolean matrices. Figures 1 and 2 present measured spanning-tree weights and matrix-vector multiplication runtimes.

M1.justification: The non-Boolean procedure is substantially revised. V1 Appendix A.3 expands rows into an Am-by-n threshold matrix and reconstructs the output afterward. V3 Appendix B.4 instead constructs an m-by-nT column-threshold matrix and transforms the query vector using successive threshold differences. The underlying Boolean MST algorithms and dynamic bucketing framework are largely retained.

E1.justification: V3 introduces actual empirical coverage through synthetic Boolean matrices generated from points and halfspaces, with ambient dimensions 2 through 12 and random real query vectors. V1 contains no corresponding original evaluation; its graph and learning applications are theoretical or supported by cited work.

E2.justification: Appendix E and Figure 2 introduce one evaluated reference method: naive NumPy matrix-vector multiplication. V1 has no original timing comparison. The additional discussion of ternary-matrix inference methods is theoretical positioning, not another experimentally evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Appendix E establishes a new evaluation protocol: fixed matrix size 4096, ambient dimension varied from 2 to 12, specified uniform sampling distributions, and measurements of MST weight and query runtime. It computes exact MSTs for implementation convenience and excludes preprocessing performance from the study. These are new experimental settings, not revisions to existing v1 experiments.

E4.justification: V3 adds a focused sensitivity analysis of how ambient dimension affects spanning-tree weight and multiplication time while matrix size stays fixed. Figures 1 and 2 investigate the proposed structural explanation; no corresponding analysis exists in v1. The study does not test the corruption guarantee.

E5.justification: V3 reports 1000 random-vector products per dimension, runtime means and standard deviations, and one-sigma error bars in Figure 2. V1 has no empirical uncertainty reporting. These are timing measurements across queries; independent matrix-generation repetitions or random seeds are not specified.

E6.justification: Figures 1 and 2 add the first original measured results: MST weights and MST-based query times generally increase with ambient dimension, while NumPy times remain comparatively stable and the runtime advantage narrows. V1 has no matching empirical results, so these are newly reported findings rather than improvements over earlier measurements.

T1.justification: Definition 2's O(n^(1-1/d)) corruptions per row become O(m^(1-1/d)) per column in Definition 1.2. Section 3.2 changes the column-tree argument to use dual VC-dimension and summed crossings rather than the previously defined maximum crossing number. Its explicit MST bound acquires log-squared dependence, supported by a new epsilon-net proof in Appendix B.2. Appendix B.4 also replaces the non-Boolean reduction's mathematical justification.

C1.justification: The main rectangular guarantee changes from O-tilde(m n^(1-1/d) + n) under v1's corruption definition to O-tilde(n m^(1-1/d) + m) under v3's revised definition. The non-Boolean guarantee is now parameterized by distinct values per column instead of the earlier threshold count. The headline square-matrix exponent and principal dynamic graph applications remain.

C2.justification: V3 explicitly states that optimal dependence on VC-dimension remains unknown without matching lower bounds, and interprets the new runtime trends through dimension dependence. Remark B.10 adds applicability to ternary neural-network inference. The concern about linear threshold-count dependence already existed in v1; its Natarajan-dimension and parsing/clique conjectures are removed.

D1.justification: V3 adds an experimental reproducibility record absent from v1: data-generation instructions, an experiment-code link, exact-MST implementation choice, Apple M4 Pro/macOS hardware with 48 GB memory, Apple Accelerate BLAS, CPU-only execution and approximately 30 minutes of total computation. V1 provides theoretical pseudocode but no comparable implementation or experimental resource information.

R1.justification: V3 consistently attributes the foundational MST algorithm to Björklund and Lingas (2001), replacing several attributions to Gasieniec and Lingas (2003); both works were already cited in v1. It adds references and connections concerning geometric multiplication, epsilon-nets, non-Boolean OMv and ternary inference, while removing some earlier citations. The overall research positioning remains.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work and technical exposition are extensively condensed and rewritten. V3 adds supplementary preliminaries, reorganizes the proof appendices, moves the tree-linearization proof out of the main text, and replaces the future-work conclusion with limitations and societal-impact paragraphs. These changes extend beyond renumbering or newly added scientific content.

P2.justification: The document is globally reformatted from the preprint layout to a conference layout, changing the title/author arrangement, text block, running headers and contents placement. V3 adds two experimental plots with axes, captions and timing error bars, and replaces the displayed threshold-encoding example. Algorithm 1 is retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the central argument by correcting v1's primal/dual VC-dimension and maximum-versus-total-crossing mismatches, adding an explicit dimension-dependent proof, and revising the non-Boolean reduction. Original timing evidence, uncertainty reporting and reproducibility information also improve assessability. The gains remain qualified: Appendix B.4 contains indexing/example inconsistencies, and the experiments cover one synthetic matrix size without measuring preprocessing.
